title: Greed and generosity

segments.voice: Yesterday, acedia, the noonday demon: the monks' heavy boredom with good things. What small task did you do when the afternoon went flat? Day one thousand two hundred five.

Every morning in the wilderness, bread is lying on the ground. The Israelites call it manna. The instruction is simple: gather what you need for today, and don't keep any till morning. Some of them keep some anyway. Just in case. A little cushion. And the next morning, in the King James words, "it bred worms, and stank." The bread that fed them, stored up, went bad overnight. And the ones who gathered a lot? The text says they had nothing left over. The ones who gathered a little had enough. Today: greed and generosity.

Greed is a closed hand. It gathers, and then it grips. It isn't always about wanting more things; often it's about fear. What if there isn't enough tomorrow? The manna story answers that fear in a strange way: the hoard doesn't protect you, and the daily gathering does. Jesus says it plainly in Luke: "Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth." Your life isn't the pile. Now watch the picture the Bible uses for the opposite. In Deuteronomy, the law turns to how people treat the poor among them, and it uses hands. Don't "shut thine hand from thy poor brother." Instead, "thou shalt open thine hand wide." Not a little. Wide. And then, much later, Paul goes back to the manna. He's collecting money for a poor church in Jerusalem, and he quotes the old story: "He that had gathered much had nothing over; and he that had gathered little had no lack." For Paul, the manna is a picture of sharing. What one has too much of, another needs, and generosity evens it out. He adds one more thing: "God loveth a cheerful giver." Cheerful. Not dutiful, not guilty. Giving that comes gladly, without counting first. So generosity isn't only about the size of a gift. It's about the shape of the hand. A closed hand can hold on to a lot, but it can't receive anything either. An open hand can let go, and it's also ready to be filled. Christians practice this in different ways, through tithes, offerings, alms, or quiet gifts nobody sees. The shape is the same.

Here's the practice: give something unplanned. Settle, and breathe. Remember the manna: enough for today, and no stockpile. Now look slowly around the room you're in, or picture your shelves, your closet, your calendar. Somewhere in there is more than you need. Let one thing come to mind you could give away today that you didn't plan to. Some money, a coat you don't wear, an hour, a book, a meal for someone. Don't weigh it too long. If you pray, you can offer it with Paul's phrase: a cheerful giver. When the bell rings, give it, as cheerfully as you can manage. The bell holds the time.
Greed and generosity. The closed hand that hoards out of fear, and the open hand that lets go and can be filled.
Your line: open hands. Today, each time you catch your hand gripping, a wallet, a phone, an hour, open it a little. Day one thousand two hundred five.

howItsDone: Christians practice generosity through tithes and offerings to their church, alms for the poor, and private giving; Christian teaching on the deadly sins pairs greed, or avarice, with generosity.

original.note: Greek: covetousness, grasping for more. The word in Luke 12:15, beware of covetousness.
